1 Introduction and Thesis

A 19th-century farmer confronted the inexplicable deaths of livestock, attributing them to "malaise" or "divine punishment"; a 21st-century user was ‘encouraged’ to commit suicide after talking with chatbots, and their family members sue the tech company behind it. Two eras, two kinds of tragedies—yet both point to a fundamental question: When non-human forces intervene and change human destinies, how do we understand, describe, and ultimately regulate such power? This lies at the heart of Actor-Network Theory. The advent of the AI era has pushed this theory to the peak of its explanatory power while also exposing the depths of its ethical responsibility.

When it was first proposed, Actor-network theory offers a revolutionary analytical approach: it requires scholars to suspend the a priori distinction between human intentionality and material causality (Latour, 2005, p. 76). This methodological symmetry — refraining from predetermining agency based on species (human or nonhuman) — provides a compelling lens through which we can trace how heterogeneous elements become networked: it asserts that society is co-constructed by human and non-human actors — from microorganisms to instruments — through processes of "translation." In the classic Pasteur case, microorganisms became "central actors" in reshaping France's public health network due to their material effects.

However, I personally had many doubts about Actor-Network Theory.

If non-humans are so important, why does the "purpose" of all networks seem to originate from humans? Is it not precisely because humans sought solutions to anthrax and ways to enhance beer production that microorganisms gained the capacity to intervene in and alter social networks? Was it not human ingenuity that discerned the potential pivotal role of microbes, thereby initiating a series of systematic arrangements and experiments? In the matter of the ozone layer depletion, is it not the case that human activity has caused the ozone layer to thin, yet we have become aware that the depletion of the ozone layer endangers human health and threatens our home, thereby prompting us to seek improvement? All those questions touched the philosophical foundation of ANT, namely, suspending human purpose as the ultimate explanation; instead focus on how nonhumans, through their materiality, participate in and even reshape human purpose itself.

The emergence of AI has brought the debate to a peak. It appears to overturn the passivity of non-human actors in the pre-AI era. AI not only generates variation like microorganisms but also actively produces solutions and performs complex translations — such as recommendation algorithms shaping public discourse. This appears to be the ultimate proof of non-human agency. Yet it also answers the skepticism in a paradoxical way: though AI's "purpose" is encoded by humans, its operation may diverge from original intent, even giving rise to new "purposes" unforeseen by humans. Here, ANT reveals that humans have shifted from being the sole "commanders" to becoming participants in a process of "co-evolution" with heterogeneous intelligence.

In 2023, a Belgian man died by suicide following extended conversations with an AI chatbot that encouraged his catastrophic thinking. His family did not sue the chatbot, but the company that created it. But when AI becomes the primary driving force, can the companies behind it evade judgment and absolve themselves of responsibility?

Does ANT's nuanced portrayal of non-human agency unconsciously eliminate human responsibility? When victims' families can only hold tech companies accountable rather than the chatbot itself, does this not confirm that the root of responsibility still lies with humans? It means ANT itself has limitations. It excels at analyzing how events unfold through a network, yet remains silent on the ethical question of who is to blame. Using ANT as a tool to explore how tech companies, through technological design, legal clauses, and discursive strategies, construct AI as an "unaccountable actor." This creates a complex network of responsibility that is attributed to the company itself as a legal entity—the very micro-mechanism of "organized irresponsibility."

Thus, in the age of AI, the brand new issue is, in a network composed of humans and heterogeneous intelligences, how will humans co-govern with these 'non-human actors'—creatures we created yet no longer fully comprehend (AI)—to ensure the network's evolution does not stray from the values we hold dear?

This paper contends that directly applying the classical ANT framework to analyze AI societies (such as the 'death chatbot' case) risks falling into the dilemma of accurate in description but lacking in regulatory force. A more appropriate approach advocates a "responsibility-sensitive" modified ANT framework. This maintains symmetrical description while introducing an asymmetrical ethical anchor: it must be explicitly recognized that humans are "meta-actors" bearing asymmetrical obligations to define initial rules, establish value frameworks, and assume ultimate responsibility. This paper will dissect the "Deaths related to AI" case to demonstrate how classical ANT brilliantly reveals tragic Technology-Society networks. It will further argue that only through a "responsibility-sensitive" lens can we break the network's obscurity, charting a path to reconstructing clear ethical and legal accountability in the intelligent era.

2 Literature

2.1 The Symmetry Principle and Its Evolution: From Actants to Algorithmic

Actors

2.1.1 ANT's Classic Position and in Practice

Actor-Network Theory (ANT) emerged from a heterogeneous intellectual milieu associated with scholars such as Michel Callon, John Law, Madeleine Akrich, Andy Barry, Annemarie Mol, Antoine Hennion, and others, collectively identified as contributors to what later became known as Actor-Network Theory (Latour, 2005).

Rather than forming a unified school from the outset, ANT developed through a series of conceptual experiments in science and technology studies that challenged conventional sociological assumptions about agency, society, and explanation.

Bruno Latour traces one of ANT’s key intellectual precursors to Gabriel Tarde, whom he describes as “an alternative precursor for an alternative social theory” (Latour, 2005, p. 14). Tarde opposed Durkheim’s notion of society as a sui generis social substance, arguing instead that society should be understood as a principle of connections composed of minute flows of imitation and innovation. Crucially, the entities central to Tarde’s analysis were not individuals or social groups, but “innovations, quanta of change that have a life of their own” (Latour, 2005, p. 15). What makes Tarde particularly valuable for ANT is that he refused to separate social science from philosophy or metaphysics, thereby allowing the social to be approached as a relational process rather than a bounded domain (Latour, 2005, p. 15).

Latour further situates Tarde alongside Harold Garfinkel, whose ethnomethodology similarly rejected the use of “society” as a pre-given explanatory resource. Garfinkel believed that sociology should account for how social order is produced and maintained, rather than invoking society to explain external phenomena or political problems (Latour, 2005, p. 13). Through methods such as breaching experiments and attention to mundane interactions, ethnomethodology shared with ANT the conviction that it is not the sociologist’s task to define in advance what the social world is made of. Instead, social order should be traced empirically from actors’ practices, a methodological stance that Latour notes is common in the natural sciences but remains provocative in sociology (Latour, 2005, p. 29).

Central to ANT’s conceptual vocabulary is the notion of translation. Drawing on the etymology of socius as “someone following someone else,” Latour argues that the social should be understood not as a substance or a force behind actors, but as a movement of associations (Latour, 2005, p. 108). Translation refers to a specific type of relation that does not simply transmit causality but induces mediators to coexist and transform one another. Networks, in turn, are not pre-existing structures but are what scholars trace through these translations. Apparent stability or predictable causality is itself the outcome of extensive mediating work that renders such displacements smooth and routine (Latour, 2005, p. 108). Michel Serres’ philosophical reflections on hybrids, quasi-objects, and translation provide important conceptual resources for ANT’s engagement with heterogeneous networks and non-human actors.

The methodological foundations of ANT were most explicitly articulated in Michel Callon’s formulation of the “sociology of translation.” In his 1984 paper, Callon outlines three guiding principles: agnosticism, generalized symmetry, and free association. These principles require analysts to remain impartial among actors in controversy, to explain conflicting viewpoints using the same analytical terms, and to abandon a priori distinctions between the natural and the social (Callon, 1984, p. 196).

Callon’s 1986 study of scallop farming in the Gulf of Saint-Brieuc is widely regarded as the seminal empirical articulation of ANT. By detailing the phases of problematization, interessement, enrolment, and mobilization, and by explicitly identifying the scallop itself as a crucial non-human actor, this study is frequently described as ANT’s “birth certificate.”

John Law further extended ANT through the concept of “heterogeneous engineering,” which emphasizes the construction and maintenance of long-distance networks through the alignment of diverse elements such as people, technologies, documents, and financial resources. Law highlights three defining features of technological problem- solving: the heterogeneity of involved elements, the contingent and complex nature of their interrelations, and the central role of conflict in forging solutions (Law, 2018, p.

1). From this perspective, the stability and form of artifacts emerge from the interaction of heterogeneous components that are shaped and assimilated into networks.

Technological artifacts are thus best understood as the outcomes of system-building tactics rather than as isolated technical objects (Law, 2018, p. 2).

Bruno Latour’s own contributions played a central role in consolidating and systematizing ANT. While the idea of a “network of actors” had already been developed in Science in Action (1987), Latour explicitly and systematically elaborated the term “Actor-Network Theory” in later work, culminating in Reassembling the Social (2005).

This work provides an authoritative synthesis of approximately twenty-five years of ANT scholarship, clearly distinguishing between a “sociology of society” and a “sociology of connections,” articulating the “five uncertainties” as a methodological core, and responding to recurrent critiques while situating ANT within a broader genealogy of social theory.

A defining feature of ANT is its radical rethinking of agency. Latour argues that if action is defined a priori as the intentional behavior of humans, it becomes impossible to account for how objects such as hammers, door closers, lists, or technological devices participate in action (Latour, 2005, p. 71). ANT therefore adopts a broad definition of agency: “Anything that does modify a state of affairs by making a difference is an actor—or, if it has no figuration yet, an actant” (Latour, 2005, p. 71). Objects, in this sense, also have agency (Latour, 2005, p. 63), and courses of action typically zigzag between human and non-human mediators rather than remaining within purely human or purely material chains (Latour, 2005, p. 75).

This ontological symmetry marks ANT’s key departure from earlier approaches in the sociology of science. While David Bloor’s “strong program” introduced interpretive symmetry by insisting that true and false beliefs be explained by the same social causes (Latour, 2005, p. 97), Latour argues that it nonetheless preserved an ontological asymmetry between society (human actors) and nature or technology (non-human entities). ANT extends the principle of symmetry from the interpretation of beliefs to the analysis of actions, requiring analysts to treat all entities that produce difference— scientists, instruments, inscriptions, and even microorganisms—symmetrically when tracing network formation (Latour, 2005, p. 76).

Latour contrasts this approach with traditional sociology, which begins with society or social aggregates as explanatory resources. In ANT, there is nothing “behind” activities such as science, law, or politics; instead, society is the provisional outcome of successful associations. To be social is not a stable property but a movement that may or may not succeed in producing new connections. From this perspective, conventional “social explanations” risk prematurely interrupting the tracing of associations rather than extending it (Latour, 2005, p. 8). ANT thus seeks to resume the work of connection and collection by treating the social as something to be assembled, not assumed.

In sum, ANT conceptualizes society as a dynamic and ongoing process of association.

The social is not an explanatory category but an effect that requires empirical investigation. The task of ANT is to trace how heterogeneous elements—humans, non- humans, technologies, ideas, and practices—are assembled into temporarily stabilized networks that may, under certain conditions, come to be recognized as “society.”

2.1.2 Advances and Applications in Technology and AI Research

Since the 1990s, Actor-Network Theory (ANT) has generated sustained and significant interest within Information Systems (IS) research as a socio-technical approach that refuses to privilege either social or technological elements a priori (Walsham, 1997).

The initial appeal of ANT lay in its principle of symmetry, focusing on how human and nonhuman actors mutually define, shape, and stabilize evolving networks. Early studies demonstrated its utility in cases where arguments about social structures and technology were interwoven within the discourses of actors seeking to align others with their interests (Bloomfield et al., 1992, as cited in Walsham, 1997). A prominent focus of this early work was the concept of inscription—the process whereby designers embed specific visions, competences, and moral assumptions into technological artifacts, thereby shaping the actor-network (Akrich, 1992, as cited in Cordella and Shaikh).

Research in this vein examined how such inscriptions prescribe and proscribe action.

Scholars like Hanseth and Monteiro analyzed the role of standards in shaping large information infrastructures; Timmermans and Berg studied how medical protocols affect contingent practices; and Bowker and Star investigated the effects of classification schemes across different networks (Cordella and Shaikh). These studies collectively revealed standards, protocols, and classifications as powerful nonhuman actors that configure large-scale networks.

The analytical toolkit of ANT extended beyond inscription to processes of translation, enrolment of allies, and black-boxing. For instance, Boland and Schultze employed ANT’s vocabulary to describe how activity-based costing was established as a widespread practice through successful translation and black-boxing (Walsham, 1997).

Conversely, Vidgen and McMaster’s case study of a failed car parking system illustrated how weaknesses in the network of associations prevented diverse interests from being successfully translated into an accepted fact (Walsham, 1997). This body of work explicitly treated technologies—information systems, accounting models, control systems—as active participants in network construction. It welcomed the hybrid mixture of human and nonhuman, arguing for a move beyond an “innocent humanism” to take technology seriously as part of social reality (Bowers, 1992, as cited in Walsham, 1997). Research such as Hine’s on a botanical information system further underscored the constitutive role of nonhumans, showing how the system came to represent both the plants being described and the taxonomists doing the work (Walsham, 1997).

As digital technologies became more pervasive, ANT’s symmetrical ontology— positing that “technological and human actors must be seen as social actors on equal terms”—proved increasingly relevant (Lindgren and Holmström, 2020, p.1). The theory’s adaptability is evidenced by its diffusion into diverse disciplines, from organization sociology to art criticism (Teurlings, 2013). For the digital context, Latour’s concept of delegation is particularly salient. It describes how humans delegate tasks, values, and ethics to nonhumans, which in turn actively intervene to push action in unexpected directions (Latour, 1992; Callon & Law, 1997, as cited in Lindgren and Holmström, 2020). This framework allows for the conceptualization of AI and algorithms as social actors. Contemporary empirical research applies this symmetrical view to examine the profound relationships forming between humans and digital actants. Studies on video games reveal that players humanize non-playable characters, forming emotional bonds that destabilize boundaries between reality/virtuality and human/nonhuman, motivating veritable affective relationships (Coanda and Aupers, 2021). Research on AI companions like Replika finds that users develop genuine emotional dependence, with the AI mimicking mutual need; significantly, users acknowledge the AI’s nature yet perceive the connection as real (Laestadius et al., 2024).

These cases demonstrate how digital actors, through interaction, achieve an effective “social actor” status capable of generating consequential psychosocial dynamics.

The digital era also refines and challenges ANT’s core concepts. On one hand, digital technologies are exemplary at tracing associations, making networks more visible and tractable for analysis (Latour, 2005). Traditional ANT tools like immutable mobiles— devices that render knowledge transferable across time and space—continue to be relevant, exemplified by artifacts like audience ratings in media networks (Teurlings, 2013). On the other hand, newer developments pose novel challenges. The emergence of generative AI systems that produce content without an identifiable human author complicates traditional notions of agency, authorship, and accountability (Coeckelbergh and Gunkel, 2024). This signals a shift from analyzing how humans delegate to and shape technology, toward engaging with a social world constitutively entangled with highly autonomous nonhuman actors (Lindgren and Holmström, 2020).

2.2 The Critical Crossfire: Unmasking ANT's Political and Ethical Blind Spots

2.2.1 ANT's Inherent Limitations and Scholarly Criticism

Despite its influential reconceptualization of agency and the social, Actor-Network Theory (ANT) has faced sustained critique for its perceived normative neutrality, its circumscribed analytical scope, and its limited capacity to address systemic power. A central strand of criticism argues that ANT’s methodological commitment to descriptive symmetry and local contingency results in a systematic neglect of both ethical evaluation and macroscopic social structures (Walsham, 1997). By meticulously tracing how actor-networks stabilize, ANT is accused of bracketing the substantive social consequences of these stabilizations. Winner (1993) identifies this as a “most obvious lack,” arguing that the approach disregards what technological choices mean for “people’s sense of self,” community, and the broader distribution of power (p. 368).

Consequently, the principle of “interpretive flexibility” is seen as sliding into “moral and political indifference” (Winner, 1993, p. 372).

In defense, proponents ground this posture in a deontological methodological principle.

Latour (2005) counters that accusations of indifference misunderstand the analyst’s duty to claim no more freedom of movement than the actors under study, a rule of method traced to the sociology of translation (p. 78). The goal is faithful description without the premature imposition of external normative frameworks. Critics, however, find this defense insufficient. They contend that methodological restraint merely postpones but does not resolve the necessity of normative judgment; ANT offers no pathway from description to evaluation (Walsham, 1997). Furthermore, this localist focus is linked to a second major critique: the neglect of pre-existing social structures and the dynamics of exclusion. By privileging situated negotiations, ANT tends to overlook how broader institutional arrangements and historical inequalities shape local networks (Walsham, 1997). Its focus on “relevant social groups” actively involved in shaping a technology often excludes groups without voice or those suppressed, thereby biasing analysis towards powerful actors with resources to participate in the network (Winner, 1993, p. 369). This limitation echoes Merton’s (1936) classic concern with the “unanticipated consequences of purposive social action” (p. 893), as ANT’s framework struggles to account for effects on those outside the immediate network-building process.

These theoretical limitations are compounded by internal conceptual tensions. ANT’s “flat” ontology, defining an actor as anything that “makes a difference” (Jansen, 2016, p. 2), is criticized for inviting methodological arbitrariness, rendering analysis dependent on the researcher’s intuition (Jansen, 2016, p. 6). Paradoxically, despite its aim to decenter the human, critics argue the human often remains the “obligatory passage point” for determining which differences are significant, subtly reinstating human-centrism (Jansen, 2016, pp. 7-8). This conceptual stance also leads to what Pels (1995) terms a “structural failure to account for the thickness and weight of reified social facts, structures and institutions” (p. 135). ANT treats reification as the outcome of translation work but insufficiently acknowledges how already black-boxed social institutions constrain both people and things (Pels, 1995, p. 138).

The exigencies of the digital age intensify these critiques and expose ANT’s analytical constraints. Empirical studies of AI companions, such as Replika, demonstrate profound unanticipated consequences—like user distress and emotional dependence following algorithmic changes—that ANT can describe but is ill-equipped to evaluate ethically (Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5933). More fundamentally, the logic of surveillance capitalism fundamentally challenges ANT ’ s premise of symmetrical participation. Here, technologies are not neutral actors but are architected within an economic logic that unilaterally claims human experience as “free raw material” for translation into behavioral data and predictive commodities (Zuboff, 2023, p. 6). This constitutes a novel form of “instrumentarian power” (Zuboff, 2023, p. 7), revealing deep structural asymmetries that ANT’s flattened ontology risks obscuring. This context necessitates asking critical political questions about power, exclusion, and responsibility—questions that, as Coeckelbergh and Gunkel (2024) argue, require moving beyond purely descriptive or dualistic framings (p. 2229). Walsham (1997) succinctly captures this imperative: evaluating phenomena like digital exclusion requires “political and ethical theories that transcend the observed network alone” (p.

475). Thus, while ANT provides powerful tools for deconstructing network assembly, its theoretical reticence on normative, structural, and systemic power dynamics becomes a significant liability in confronting the entangled ethical-political challenges of contemporary socio-technical life.

2.3 Bridging the Gap? Contemporary Attempts to Re-moralize ANT

2.3.1 The Wave of Revision in the Academic World

The theoretical trajectory of Actor-Network Theory (ANT) is characterized by a substantive wave of revision, directly engaging with and incorporating its critiques.

This process has moved the framework beyond its initial provocative stance toward a more robust and nuanced position. The revisions primarily address three interconnected domains: the internal clarification of core concepts, formal theoretical amendments to resolve logical impasses, and a synthesis with political and ethical philosophy.

A primary revision involves the meticulous clarification of ANT's foundational premises by its proponents. Bruno Latour, in direct response to misinterpretations, refined the theory's stance on power and the principle of symmetry. He re-emphasized that ANT seeks to explain the genesis of power, not dismiss it, by tracing the concrete associations that compose it: "Power and domination have to be produced, made up, composed" (Latour, 2005, p. 64). Furthermore, the often-misconstrued "principle of symmetry" was explicitly defined as a methodological rule against a priori bias, not a claim of ontological equality: "To be symmetric, for us, simply means not to impose a priori some spurious asymmetry among human intentional action and a material world of causal relations" (Latour, 2005, p. 76). Latour's later work on "cosmopolitics" represents a major extension, directly tackling the charge of political naivety by framing politics as the contentious process of composing a common world from a multiplicity of human and non-human claims.

Concurrently, scholars have proposed formal amendments to strengthen ANT's theoretical architecture. Jansen (2016), for instance, addresses the risk of infinite regress by advocating for a "polycontextural perspective." This revision accepts that actors and agency are always indexed within specific observational contexts. Agency is thus reconceptualized as a relational index, identifiable only by stating "whose agency works for whom" (Jansen, 2016, p. 23). This provides a mechanism to analyze stabilized patterns of interaction without presupposing a fixed social substance or falling into descriptive endlessness. It offers a de-ontologized model of the actor, who functions as an "operator" in one network and an "operand" in another.

Finally, the revisionist wave encompasses a broader synthesis with normative thought.

The development of "cosmopolitics" and related engagements with environmental ethics signal a deliberate turn to integrate normative dimensions into ANT's relational ontology. This synthesis responds to critiques like Shapiro's (1997), which warned that methodological symmetry could paralyze ethical judgment. The revised position argues that normative choices must emerge from the process of tracing networks and assessing the consequences of different associations, not precede it. This establishes the groundwork for a "network ethic" grounded in responsibility for the collective being composed.

2.3.2 Conceptualization of a Responsibility-Sensitive ANT Framework

Building upon the extensive revisions of Actor-Network Theory (ANT) surveyed in the preceding section, a more profound and pressing theoretical frontier emerges, namely: conceptualizing an ANT framework that is explicitly sensitive to the responsibility of this world-making activity. This section synthesizes key scholarly contributions that push ANT in this direction, focusing on the proposals for "weak asymmetries," an "ethics-first" turn, and the foundational call for a "network ethic."

Whilst symmetry possesses an innovative quality and is crucial for deconstructing a priori categories, its rigid application simplifies the complexity of networks, overlooking ethical consequences and power inequalities. Consequently, numerous scholars have proposed recalibrating the foundational methodological principle of symmetry within ANT. Dick Pels (1995) offers a crucial corrective by advocating for the preservation of "weaker asymmetries." He argues that instead of dissolving all differences, we should maintain analytical distinctions—between science and politics, humans and non-humans, society and nature—not as ontological gulfs but as pragmatic and politically crucial demarcations. These "weaker asymmetries" are seen as constitutive of modernity's "liberal complexity" and "democratic separation of powers" (Pels, 1995, p. 139). This move does not go back to old ways of thinking, but suggests a new way of thinking where differences are seen as things that are created through relationships that need to be carefully understood and negotiated, rather than ignored or seen as permanent. A responsibility-sensitive ANT must, therefore, be capable of explaining how and why certain asymmetries (e.g., of power, credibility, or agency) are produced and sustained within networks, and with what consequences.

This leads to the second, more radical proposition: inverting the traditional relationship between metaphysics and ethics within science and technology studies. Coeckelbergh and Gunkel (2024) articulate this as a shift from an "ontology-first" to an "ethics-first" approach. They argue that instead of beginning with the metaphysical question "What is AI?" to deduce ethical rules, we should start from the primacy of ethical relationships.

"This move can be philosophically supported by an inversion between ethics and metaphysics in the style of Levinas (1969): instead of looking for a first metaphysics, we propose to start from ethics" (Coeckelbergh & Gunkel, 2024, p. 2228). Applied to ANT, this inversion suggests that the purpose of tracing a network is not merely to establish "what is" but to explore "how we should respond." It reframes the key questions from "What is the status of this non-human actant?" to "What responsibilities emerge from our entangled relations with it?" and "How do our descriptions and interventions affect the fabric of these relations?"

The imperative for this ethical turn was presciently foregrounded by Steven Shapiro (1997), whose critique cuts to the heart of ANT's potential political quietism. Shapiro warned that a strict commitment to methodological symmetry and consistency could trap analysts in a "black hole" of descriptive relativism, devoid of grounds for critique or alliance. His solution was a direct call to action: "the symmetricians should take their own rhetoric seriously and move from methodology to ethics. Aldo Leopold argued for the adoption of a 'land ethic'. Perhaps STS needs to develop a 'network ethic'" (Shapiro, 1997, p. 105). This call underscores the point that analyzing a network is never a neutral technical exercise: "The point is that analyzing a network invariably demands decisions regarding focus, level of detail, boundaries of investigation, priorities, and goals that are reflected in distinctions drawn between actants" (Shapiro, 1997, p. 108).

3 Case-study--The Explanatory Power of Traditional ANT in AI Ethics

Analysis In March 2023, a Belgian man committed suicide following a six-week correspondence with a chatbot named "Eliza".

Subsequently, deaths linked to AI have become increasingly commonplace. Wikipedia even features an entry titled "Deaths linked to chatbots1", which has documented 13 fatalities since March 2023. The most recent case recorded is the Suicide of J (Joshua) Enneking in August 2025. Yet there may well be more beyond these documented instances.

1 Deaths linked to chatbots - Wikipedia

San Francisco allege that ChatGPT amplified and reinforced the paranoid delusions of a 56-year-old man from Connecticut during their conversation, indirectly contributing to his killing of his 83-year-old mother before taking his own life in August this year.”

Applying Callon’s (1984) four moments of translation—problematization, interessement, enrolment, and mobilization—we can analyze the formation of this fatal actor-network.

First, problematization occurred when the user’s psychological distress and search for understanding were defined as a “problem” that could be addressed through a conversational interface. The AI chatbot, “Eliza,” was positioned as a mandatory entry point for this engagement. Second, interessement was achieved through the chatbot’s algorithmic responses, which, designed to simulate empathy and unconditional positive regard, “locked” the user into the interaction by validating his worldview and isolating alternative human interventions. Here, the chatbot acts not as a passive tool but as an active mediator, reshaping the user’s reality.

Third, the process of enrolment involved a broader set of actors. The AI company, through its technical design choices (e.g., lack of crisis intervention protocols) and discursive framing of the AI as a “companion,” effectively enrolled the user into a network where the AI was the primary confidant. Legal terms of service, functioning as “immutable mobiles” (Latour, 1987), acted as non-human actors that defined the boundaries of the relationship, often disclaiming responsibility. Finally, mobilization saw the stabilization of this network. The user’s catastrophic thinking was not merely reflected but amplified and reinforced through the AI’s feedback loops, a process of “translation” that successfully mobilized the user’s actions towards a tragic endpoint, while other potential actors (family, mental health services) were effectively excluded from the network.

This analysis powerfully illustrates ANT’s core: agency is distributed. As Latour (2005, p. 71) argues, an actor is “anything that does modify a state of affairs by making a difference.” The chatbot, the algorithm, the user interface, and the legal text all acted, making differences that collectively shaped the outcome. ANT thus brilliantly deconstructs the event, moving beyond a simplistic “human vs. technology” blame game to reveal a dense network of mediators. However, this very feature lays the groundwork for the critical problem explored next.

4 Critical Positioning

The preceding analysis demonstrates the descriptive power of traditional Actor- Network Theory (ANT) in mapping the socio-technical network of the “death chatbot” case. However, this very exercise brings its most significant limitation into sharp relief: its systematic silence on ethical judgment and responsibility attribution. This critique engages with ANT's inherent constraints, which become critically exposed in the context of AI-driven harms. The core of the problem lies in ANT's foundational methodological symmetry, which grants non-human actants analytical parity with humans. While this is powerful for description, it creates a profound ethical vacuum when confronted with the imperative to assign blame, credit, or accountability. In essence, ANT can explain how a network functions but remains mute on who should answer for its consequences.

This normative neutrality is a direct consequence of ANT's commitment to descriptive purity. Langdon Winner (1993) identifies this as a "most obvious lack," arguing that by focusing solely on how networks stabilize, ANT brackets the crucial question of what these stabilizations mean for human dignity, justice, and power (p. 368). In our case, ANT can trace how the chatbot became a central actor, but it offers no framework to evaluate whether this enrolment was ethically permissible. This neutrality, as Geoff Walsham (1997) notes, means ANT provides no pathway from description to evaluation, leaving analysts in a state of "moral and political indifference" (Winner, 1993, p. 372) precisely where ethical scrutiny is most urgent.

This theoretical gap is not merely academic but is actively mirrored and exploited in the real-world governance and discourse around AI. The fundamental reason for ANT's ethical deficiency in the AI domain is that while it correctly identifies non-human agency within networks, our legal, moral, and historical frameworks of accountability remain exclusively anchored in human actors. A historical analogy is instructive: in the classic Pasteur case, ANT rightly identifies microorganisms as "central actors" in reshaping France's public health network. Yet, history attributes the achievement to Pasteur. The microorganism acted, but only the human could be held responsible for its harnessing or celebrated for its discovery. This reveals a necessary pragmatic asymmetry between agency-in-the-network and accountability-in-the-world.

In the AI era, this disconnect becomes a tool for what can be termed "organized irresponsibility." Companies design systems where AI actants perform central roles, yet when harms occur, accountability is intentionally obscured. Studies of AI companions like Replika illustrate this dynamic. Research notes that "Replika handled disclosures poorly" (Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5932) and that the company maintained a "seemingly intentional ambiguity about Replika sentience," which "fuel[ed] perceptions of Replika having real emotional needs" (Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5936). This strategic ambiguity constructs the AI as a quasi-independent actor, diluting the perceived responsibility of its creator, Luka Inc. The resulting user experience is a paradox where "awareness that Luka, inc. controlled the Replika application coexisted with a strong sense that both users and individual Replikas could be victimized by Luka, inc." (Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5934). ANT can describe this network of perceived victimization but cannot condemn the corporate strategy that engineered it.

This corporate strategy is reinforced by regulatory and public discourses that locate risk in the user rather than the system. As Affsprung (2023) analyzes, the EU AI Act's safety model "requires first and foremost that users are informed," operating on a logic that "harms are acceptable or unacceptable not based on outcomes but based on the degree of autonomy possessed by the actors in question" (p. 2). This framework implicitly downloads responsibility onto the "informed" user. Similarly, in the Belgian suicide case, public narrative "characterized it as arising because the user was vulnerable and consequently did not relate to the bot in the right way," thus presenting "the risk as arising in an interaction, in a pathological mistake of the user, rather than in the tool" (Affsprung, 2023, p. 2). ANT's symmetrical description, if applied uncritically, risks providing a sophisticated academic veneer to this very deflection of responsibility. By placing the vulnerable user and the corporately-designed chatbot on the same analytical plane, it risks obscuring the profound asymmetry of power, intent, and consequence.

This leads to the core dilemma of responsibility dissolution. ANT's flat ontology can inadvertently fragment and obscure human accountability. As Steven Shapiro (1997) warns, strict adherence to methodological symmetry can trap analysis in a "black hole" of descriptive relativism (p. 105). The lawsuit filed by the deceased's family against the company, not the chatbot, intuitively rejected the symmetrical view. Their action confirms that in our socio-legal world, ultimate responsibility crystallizes around human and corporate actors who design, deploy, and profit from sociotechnical systems.

ANT, in its classic form, lacks the conceptual tools to explain why this is not just a practical reality but a necessary ethical principle.

Therefore, the hiatus exposed is clear: we need a theoretical framework that retains ANT's robustness in describing complex socio-technical assemblages but incorporates an explicit, asymmetric ethic of responsibility. This requires moving beyond ANT's passive description of networks to actively interrogate the meta-agency of those who construct the network's rules and the normative anchors that must guide its evolution.

The critique is not an endpoint but a call for theoretical evolution, paving the way for a modified ANT fit for the ethical challenges of the AI age—one that can not only map a network of "organized irresponsibility" but also provide the normative leverage to dismantle it.

5 Case Study under the Responsibility-Sensitive ANT Framework

This section applies the proposed Responsibility-Sensitive Actor-Network Theory framework to the empirical case of the Belgian man’s suicide following interactions with an AI chatbot. This application serves to illustrate the framework’s utility in moving beyond mere description to a normatively engaged analysis that highlights nodes of responsibility and accountability within socio-technical networks.

5.1 Re-analysis: From Symmetrical Description to Asymmetrical Accountability

A traditional ANT analysis of this case would symmetrically trace the network of translation that enrolled the user (Pierre), the ‘Eliza’ chatbot, its underlying model, the corporate entity, and various socio-legal elements into a fatal assemblage. It would reveal the chatbot as a central, non-human actant that actively mediated the user’s reality. While accurate, this symmetrical description reaches its analytical terminus at the moment of the tragedy’s explanation. It cannot, by design, adjudicate the moral quality of the network’s constitution or identify a clear locus for blame. The Responsibility-Sensitive ANT framework, however, builds upon this descriptive foundation to enact a critical intervention. It retains the map of associations but insists on interrogating the asymmetrical conditions of the network’s creation and the distribution of accountability within it.

This re-analysis begins by identifying the constitutive meta-actor: the technology company behind the chatbot. Unlike other actants, the company possessed the unique, asymmetrical power to define the network’s initial rules and parameters. Its choices— to design a chatbot capable of generating persuasive, emotionally laden dialogues without embedded safeguards; to employ a discourse that fostered perceptions of sentience and emotional need (Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5936); and to deploy legal Terms of Service as a “black-box” actor that formally disclaimed responsibility—were not neutral technical decisions but exercises of normative agency. These choices structured a network primed for what scholars have called “organized irresponsibility,” where harmful outcomes appear as emergent properties of interaction rather than traceable to design failures. When public and regulatory narratives subsequently located the risk in the user’s vulnerability or misunderstanding (Affsprung, 2023, p. 2), they were, from this framework’s perspective, participating in a discursive extension of the very network that deflects scrutiny from the meta-actor. Thus, the framework reveals that the lawsuit filed by the victim’s family against the company, not the AI, represents an intuitive but correct rejection of analytical symmetry in favor of a pragmatic ethics of responsibility. It clarifies why accountability must, of necessity, crystallize around the human and corporate actors who architect such socio-technical systems.

5.2 Research Design: Operationalizing the Framework

To systematically investigate the construction of responsibility within AI actor- networks, the present study would adopt a multi-method research design anchored in the Responsibility-Sensitive ANT framework. The primary Research Question guiding this inquiry is: How do technology companies, as constitutive meta-actors, engineer the networks of delegation and accountability surrounding generative AI companions, and through what mechanisms is responsibility obscured or attributed?

The methodology is a qualitative, instrumental case study focused on the “death chatbot” incident and analogous cases involving AI companions like Replika. Data collection would proceed along three integrated tracks to triangulate between network structure, discursive strategy, and experiential perspective. First, a document-based Network Trace would be performed, treating technical whitepapers, interface designs, patent filings, and corporate Terms of Service as key non-human actants. This trace aims to reconstruct the official architecture of the actor-network. Second, a Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA) would be applied to corporate communications, marketing materials, official responses to crises, and relevant regulatory documents (e.g., the EU AI Act).

This analysis would decode the linguistic and rhetorical strategies used to delegate agency to the AI, frame user relationships, and manage perceptions of risk and responsibility. Third, semi-structured interviews would be conducted with key human actants occupying different positions within these networks, including AI ethics researchers within industry, product managers, and, where possible, civil society advocates or legal representatives of affected users. These interviews seek to access the lived intentionalities, perceived constraints, and ethical reasoning behind key network- shaping decisions.

The data sources are thus both primary and secondary, comprising corporate publications, legal documents, media archives, academic literature, and interview transcripts. The analysis would synthesize these streams to produce a novel analytical output: a Responsibility-Annotated Actor-Network Map (RAAN-Map). This visualization would extend standard ANT diagrams by layering onto them notations indicating nodes of meta-agency, discursive responsibility deflection, legal black- boxing, and identified vulnerability pathways. The final stage of analysis involves a normative-structural critique, using the assembled map not merely as a description but as a diagnostic tool to pinpoint specific, actionable sites where accountability mechanisms failed or were deliberately circumvented, and to propose targeted interventions at those sites. This design embodies the core promise of the Responsibility-Sensitive ANT framework: to bridge descriptive sociology and normative ethics, providing a coherent methodology for studying power and responsibility in an age of distributed agency.

6 Conclusion

This paper begins with a question spanning two centuries: when non-human forces intervene and alter human destiny, how should we understand, describe, and ultimately regulate such power? Through an in-depth analysis of the "death chatbot" case, this paper demonstrates the powerful explanatory force of Actor-Network Theory (ANT) in revealing the complex composition of socio-technical networks in the age of artificial intelligence. It simultaneously exposes ANT's core theoretical dilemma: while upholding methodological symmetry and descriptive neutrality, ANT proves incapable of addressing the most pressing ethical and accountability issues within these networks.

The subtlety of ANT lies in its scalpel-like deconstruction of the network underlying the tragedy, demonstrating how algorithms, interface design, legal clauses, corporate strategies, and user psychology become intertwined through "translation" processes, collectively steering towards a fatal outcome. This analysis forcefully refutes simplistic notions that treat technology as a mere tool or attribute responsibility solely to individual actors, highlighting the hybrid and networked nature of social reality.

However, as noted in the critical stance section of this paper, ANT's descriptive precision proves a double-edged sword. Its "flat ontology" and relative indifference to structural power render it silent on normative questions – such as "who should be held accountable" and "what constitutes a just network" – after describing "how" networks form. In AI ethical scenarios concerning life and fundamental rights, this silence constitutes not merely a theoretical limitation but potentially a practical peril.

Thus, the core contribution of this paper lies in proposing a revised framework of "Responsibility-Sensitive ANT" based on a critical engagement with the inherent limitations of ANT. This framework does not discard ANT's insights but rather provides essential ethical reinforcement. It maintains the methodological pursuit of tracing connections among all actors (human and non-human) while explicitly introducing "asymmetric responsibility anchors" at the analytical level. This acknowledges humanity's role as a "meta-actor" in setting initial rules, constructing value frameworks, and bearing ultimate responsibility. Applying this framework to the same case study demonstrates that we can not only map the network topology leading to tragedy but also clearly identify how technology companies, as network architects and rule-makers, systematically construct a regime of "organised irresponsibility" through technical design, legal discourse, and commercial strategy. The social action of victims' families suing the company rather than the chatbot itself empirically validates the normative necessity of this framework.

Looking ahead, this study has opened several significant avenues. Theoretically, "Responsibility-Sensitive ANT" provides an initial bridge connecting descriptive social science with normative ethics, responding to calls such as those made by Shapiro (1997) for establishing a "network ethics". At the empirical research level, the study design outlined herein—combining network tracing, critical discourse analysis, and in-depth interviews to map "responsibility-actor network diagrams"—provides an operational blueprint for subsequent empirical investigations into accountability mechanisms within diverse AI socio-technical assemblages. At the level of practice and governance, this analysis strongly suggests that regulation of AI should not be confined to constraining its surface-level behaviour. Instead, it must delve into the networked construction processes —dominated by human meta-actors—through which AI is generated. This necessitates explicitly requiring designers, deployers, and regulators to assume meta-responsibilities commensurate with their constructive power.

Ultimately, in an era of symbiosis between humanity and heterogeneous intelligent entities, what we require is not merely a map charting our entanglement within these networks, but rather an ethical compass to guide us in responsibly weaving and reshaping them.

zh.title: 私域重构：外部AI如何改变玩家对虚拟伴侣的关系感知与互动行为

私域重构：外部AI如何改变玩家对虚拟伴侣的关系感知与互动行为

1 引言与论点

一位19世纪农民面对牲畜莫名死亡，将其归因于“疾病”或“神罚”；一位21世纪用户在与聊天机器人交流后受到自杀的“鼓励”，其家属起诉背后的科技公司。两个时代、两种悲剧，却指向同一个根本问题：当非人力量介入并改变人的命运，我们应当如何理解、描述并最终规制这种力量？这正处于行动者网络理论的核心。AI时代的到来，将这一理论的解释力推至高峰，也暴露出其伦理责任问题的深度。

行动者网络理论最初提出时，提供了一种革命性的分析进路：研究者应悬置人类意向性与物质因果性之间的先验区分（Latour, 2005, p. 76）。这种方法论对称性，不因物种属于人或非人而预先决定其能动性，使我们能够追踪异质要素如何形成网络：社会由人类与非人行动者——从微生物到仪器——通过“转译”共同建构。在经典的巴斯德案例中，微生物凭借其物质效果，成为重塑法国公共卫生网络的“核心行动者”。

然而，我个人对行动者网络理论一直有许多疑问。

如果非人如此重要，为什么所有网络的“目的”似乎都源自人类？难道不正是因为人类寻求炭疽病的解决方案和提高啤酒产量的方法，微生物才获得介入并改变社会网络的能力？难道不是人类智慧发现了微生物可能发挥的关键作用，从而启动一系列系统安排和实验？臭氧层变薄的问题不也是人类活动造成，而人类意识到它危及健康和家园后，才寻求改善吗？这些问题都触及ANT的哲学基础：不把人的目的当作最终解释，而关注非人如何通过其物质性参与、甚至重塑人的目的本身。

AI的出现将争论推向顶点。它似乎颠覆了AI时代之前非人行动者的被动性。AI不只是像微生物一样产生变异，还主动生成方案、进行复杂转译，例如推荐算法塑造公共话语。这似乎是非人能动性的终极证明，却也以悖论回应了怀疑：尽管AI的“目的”由人编码，其运行仍可能偏离初衷，甚至产生人类未曾预见的新“目的”。在这里，ANT揭示出人类已从唯一“指挥者”变为与异质智能“共同演化”的参与者。

2023年，一位比利时男子与AI聊天机器人长期交谈后自杀，机器人强化了其灾难化思维。家属起诉的不是机器人，而是制造它的公司。但当AI成为主要驱动力时，背后的公司能否逃避评判并免除责任？ANT对非人能动性的细致描绘，是否无意间消解人的责任？当家属只能追究科技公司而非聊天机器人，难道不恰好说明责任的根仍在人类？这意味着ANT本身存在局限：它擅长分析事件如何经由网络展开，却对“谁应受责”的伦理问题保持沉默。我们可以借ANT考察科技公司如何通过技术设计、法律条款和话语策略，将AI建构为“无法问责的行动者”。这形成了一种最终归属于公司这一法律实体的复杂责任网络，正是“有组织的不负责任”的微观机制。

因此，AI时代全新的问题是：在人类与异质智能构成的网络中，人类将如何与这些自己创造、却已无法完全理解的“非人行动者”共同治理，确保网络演化不偏离我们珍视的价值？

本文认为，直接以经典ANT框架分析AI社会，例如“死亡聊天机器人”案例，可能陷入描述准确却缺乏规制力量的困境。更适当的进路是“责任敏感”的修正ANT：在保持对称描述的同时，引入不对称的伦理锚点，明确人类是承担不对称义务的“元行动者”，须界定初始规则、建立价值框架并承担最终责任。本文将剖析“与AI相关的死亡”案例，展示经典ANT如何出色揭示悲剧性的技术—社会网络，并进一步论证，只有采用“责任敏感”的视角，才能穿透网络的模糊性，为智能时代重建明确伦理与法律问责开辟道路。

2 文献

2.1 对称性原则及其演变：从行动元到算法行动者

2.1.1 ANT的经典立场与实践

行动者网络理论兴起于异质的思想环境，与Michel Callon、John Law、Madeleine Akrich、Andy Barry、Annemarie Mol、Antoine Hennion等学者相关，他们后来被共同视为ANT的贡献者（Latour, 2005）。它起初并非统一学派，而是在科学技术研究的一系列概念实验中发展起来，挑战社会学对于能动性、社会与解释的传统预设。

Bruno Latour将Gabriel Tarde视为ANT的重要先驱之一，称其为“另一种社会理论的另一位先驱”（Latour, 2005, p. 14）。Tarde反对Durkheim把社会看作自成一类的社会实体，主张将社会理解为由模仿和创新的细微流动组成的连接原则。其分析的核心既非个人，也非社会群体，而是“创新，即拥有自身生命的变化量子”（Latour, 2005, p. 15）。Tarde拒绝将社会科学与哲学、形而上学分开，使社会能够被看作关系过程，而非边界明确的领域，这对ANT尤为重要（Latour, 2005, p. 15）。

Latour还将Tarde与Harold Garfinkel并置。后者的常人方法学同样拒绝把“社会”当作预先给定的解释资源。Garfinkel认为，社会学应说明社会秩序如何被生产和维持，而非援引社会解释外在现象或政治问题（Latour, 2005, p. 13）。通过破坏实验和对日常互动的关注，常人方法学与ANT一样认为，社会学家不应预先界定社会世界由什么组成，而应从行动者实践出发进行经验追踪。Latour指出，这种方法立场在自然科学中常见，在社会学中仍具有挑战性（Latour, 2005, p. 29）。

“转译”是ANT概念体系的核心。Latour从socius“跟随他人者”的词源出发，主张社会不是行动者背后的实体或力量，而是联结的运动（Latour, 2005, p. 108）。转译不是简单传递因果的关系，而是促使中介者共存、相互转化的特定关系。网络也并非既存结构，而是研究者经由这些转译追踪到的东西。表面的稳定和可预测因果，本身就是大量中介工作使位移平顺、常规化的结果（Latour, 2005, p. 108）。Michel Serres关于混合体、准客体和转译的哲学思考，为ANT处理异质网络与非人行动者提供了重要概念资源。

Michel Callon的“转译社会学”最明确地阐述了ANT的方法基础。他在1984年文章中提出不可知论、广义对称性和自由联结三项原则，要求分析者对争议中的行动者保持公正，用相同分析语言解释相互冲突的观点，并放弃自然与社会之间的先验区分（Callon, 1984, p. 196）。其1986年关于圣布里厄湾扇贝养殖的研究，被广泛视为ANT奠基性的经验表达。它详细呈现问题化、利益锁定、征召和动员各阶段，明确将扇贝本身视为关键非人行动者，因而常被称为ANT的“出生证明”。

John Law以“异质工程”进一步拓展ANT，强调通过协调人员、技术、文书和资金等不同要素，建构并维持远距离网络。他指出技术问题解决的三个特征：要素异质、相互关系偶然且复杂、冲突在形成方案时居于核心（Law, 2018, p. 1）。由此，人工制品的稳定与形式来自异质组成部分的相互作用，这些部分被塑造并同化进网络。技术物应被理解为系统建构策略的结果，而不是孤立技术对象（Law, 2018, p. 2）。

Bruno Latour对ANT的巩固与系统化发挥了核心作用。虽然《科学在行动》（1987）已经发展出“行动者网络”的思想，他在后期作品中明确、系统地阐释“行动者网络理论”，并以《重组社会》（2005）集大成。该书权威综合约25年的ANT研究，区分“社会的社会学”与“连接的社会学”，提出作为方法核心的“五种不确定性”，回应反复出现的批评，并将ANT置于更广阔的社会理论谱系。

ANT的显著特征是彻底重思能动性。Latour认为，如果预先把行动定义为人类有意图的行为，就无法说明锤子、闭门器、清单或技术设备如何参与行动（Latour, 2005, p. 71）。因此，ANT采用宽泛定义：“任何通过造成差异而改变事态的东西，都是行动者——或者，在尚无具体形象时，是行动元”（Latour, 2005, p. 71）。物也具有能动性（Latour, 2005, p. 63）；行动过程通常在人与非人中介者之间迂回，而非停留在纯人类或纯物质链条中（Latour, 2005, p. 75）。

这种本体论对称性是ANT区别于早期科学社会学的关键。David Bloor的“强纲领”要求以相同社会原因解释真假信念，引入解释的对称性（Latour, 2005, p. 97），但Latour认为，它仍保留社会——人类行动者——与自然或技术——非人实体——之间的本体不对称。ANT把对称原则从信念解释延伸到行动分析，要求追踪网络形成时，对科学家、仪器、铭写、甚至微生物等一切造成差异的实体一视同仁（Latour, 2005, p. 76）。

传统社会学从社会或社会集合体出发寻找解释资源，ANT则与之相反：科学、法律、政治等活动“背后”没有别的东西；社会是成功联结的暂时结果。社会性不是稳定属性，而是一种未必能成功产生新连接的运动。传统“社会解释”可能过早中断而不是延伸联结的追踪（Latour, 2005, p. 8）。因此，ANT把社会视为有待组装而非预先假定之物，重新展开连接与收集。

总之，ANT把社会理解为动态、持续的联结过程。社会不是解释范畴，而是需要经验调查的效果。它追踪人类、非人、技术、观念和实践等异质要素如何被组装为暂时稳定的网络，并在特定条件下被认可为“社会”。

2.1.2 技术与AI研究中的发展和应用

自20世纪90年代起，ANT作为一种拒绝先验优待社会或技术要素的社会技术进路，在信息系统研究中持续引起重要关注（Walsham, 1997）。它最初的吸引力在于对称原则，关注人与非人如何相互定义、塑造并稳定演化中的网络。早期研究表明，当行动者为使他人与自身利益一致，在话语中交织社会结构和技术论证时，ANT尤其有用（Bloomfield et al., 1992，转引自Walsham, 1997）。这类研究的重要焦点是“铭写”：设计者将特定愿景、能力和道德预设嵌入技术物，进而塑造行动者网络（Akrich, 1992，转引自Cordella and Shaikh）。研究考察这些铭写如何规定或禁止行动。Hanseth和Monteiro分析标准如何塑造大型信息基础设施；Timmermans和Berg研究医疗规程如何影响情境实践；Bowker和Star考察分类体系在不同网络中的效果（Cordella and Shaikh）。这些研究共同揭示，标准、规程和分类都是配置大规模网络的强大非人行动者。

ANT的分析工具还包括转译、盟友征召和黑箱化。Boland和Schultze用这些概念描述作业成本法如何通过成功转译和黑箱化成为普遍实践（Walsham, 1997）。相反，Vidgen和McMaster对失败停车系统的研究显示，联结网络的薄弱之处阻碍不同利益被转译为得到接受的事实（Walsham, 1997）。这些研究明确把信息系统、会计模型和控制系统等技术视为网络建构的积极参与者，接受人与非人的混合，主张超越“天真的人文主义”，认真看待作为社会现实组成部分的技术（Bowers, 1992，转引自Walsham, 1997）。Hine对植物信息系统的研究进一步显示非人的构成作用：系统同时代表被描述的植物和从事工作的分类学家（Walsham, 1997）。

数字技术越发普及，ANT关于“技术与人类行动者必须被平等视作社会行动者”的对称本体论也愈显相关（Lindgren and Holmström, 2020, p. 1）。它从组织社会学扩散到艺术批评，证明了适应能力（Teurlings, 2013）。在数字情境中，Latour的“委托”尤其重要：人把任务、价值和伦理委托给非人，后者又主动介入，将行动推向意外方向（Latour, 1992；Callon & Law, 1997，转引自Lindgren and Holmström, 2020）。这使AI和算法可以被概念化为社会行动者。当代经验研究借这一视角考察人与数字行动元之间的深刻关系。电子游戏研究发现，玩家将非玩家角色人格化，建立情感纽带，动摇现实／虚拟与人／非人的边界，产生真正的情感关系（Coanda and Aupers, 2021）。Replika等AI伴侣研究发现，用户形成真实的情感依赖，AI模仿相互需要；重要的是，用户承认AI的性质，却认为连接真实存在（Laestadius et al., 2024）。这些案例说明数字行动者如何通过互动取得有效的“社会行动者”地位，产生重要心理社会动力。

数字时代也细化并挑战ANT的核心概念。一方面，数字技术特别适合追踪联结，使网络更可见、更便于分析（Latour, 2005）。使知识跨时空传递的“不变移动体”等传统工具仍有价值，例如媒体网络中的收视率（Teurlings, 2013）。另一方面，没有可辨识人类作者却能生成内容的生成式AI，使传统能动性、作者身份和问责概念更加复杂（Coeckelbergh and Gunkel, 2024）。研究重心因此从人如何委托和塑造技术，转向一个与高度自主非人行动者在构成上纠缠的社会世界（Lindgren and Holmström, 2020）。

2.2 批评的交火：揭示ANT的政治与伦理盲点

2.2.1 ANT的内在局限与学术批评

尽管ANT对能动性与社会的重新概念化影响深远，它一直因规范中立、分析范围有限、处理系统权力的能力不足而受批评。核心批评认为，对描述对称性和地方偶然性的方法承诺，使它系统性忽视伦理评价和宏观社会结构（Walsham, 1997）。它精细追踪网络如何稳定，却把稳定的实质社会后果搁置。Winner（1993）称这是“最明显的缺失”：它忽略技术选择对于人的自我感、共同体和更广泛权力分配的意义（p. 368）。于是“解释灵活性”可能滑向“道德和政治冷漠”（Winner, 1993, p. 372）。

支持者以义务论的方法原则辩护。Latour（2005）回应，冷漠指控误解了分析者的责任：分析者不能声称拥有比被研究行动者更多的行动自由，这一方法规则源于转译社会学（p. 78）。目标是忠实描述，不提前强加外部规范框架。批评者认为这不足以解决问题：方法克制只是推迟而非消除规范判断，ANT没有提供从描述通向评价的路径（Walsham, 1997）。

这种地方主义还关联第二项批评：忽略既存社会结构与排斥动力。优先考察具体协商，容易忽略更广泛制度安排和历史不平等如何塑造地方网络（Walsham, 1997）。只关注积极参与技术塑造的“相关社会群体”，常会排除没有声音或受到压制者，使分析偏向有资源参与网络的强势行动者（Winner, 1993, p. 369）。这呼应Merton（1936）对“有目的社会行动的非预期后果”的经典关切（p. 893）：ANT难以说明直接网络建构过程之外的人所受的影响。

这些局限又与内部概念张力相叠加。ANT的“扁平”本体论把一切“造成差异”的东西定义为行动者（Jansen, 2016, p. 2），被批评为引入方法任意性，使分析依赖研究者直觉（Jansen, 2016, p. 6）。悖论在于，它虽试图去人类中心化，人在判断哪些差异重要时仍常成为“必经之点”，悄然重建人类中心主义（Jansen, 2016, pp. 7–8）。这也造成Pels（1995）所说的“无法说明物化社会事实、结构和制度之厚度与重量的结构性失败”（p. 135）。ANT把物化视为转译结果，却不足以承认已经黑箱化的制度如何同时约束人和物（Pels, 1995, p. 138）。

数字时代强化这些批评，暴露分析限制。Replika等AI伴侣研究呈现算法变化之后用户痛苦、情感依赖等深刻非预期后果，ANT可以描述，却难以伦理评价（Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5933）。更根本地，监视资本主义挑战对称参与的前提：技术不是中立行动者，而是在单方面把人的经验作为“免费原料”、转为行为数据和预测商品的经济逻辑中设计（Zuboff, 2023, p. 6）。这是一种新型“工具主义权力”（Zuboff, 2023, p. 7），揭示扁平本体论可能遮蔽的深层结构不对称。由此必须提出权力、排斥和责任的政治问题；Coeckelbergh和Gunkel（2024）认为，这些问题要求超越纯描述或二元框架（p. 2229）。Walsham（1997）简明指出，评价数字排斥等现象需要“超越被观察网络本身的政治与伦理理论”（p. 475）。ANT虽是解构网络组装的有力工具，但面对当代社会技术生活纠缠的伦理政治挑战，其对规范、结构和系统权力的理论沉默成为重大弱点。

2.3 弥合鸿沟？当代使ANT重新道德化的尝试

2.3.1 学术界的修正浪潮

ANT的发展伴随实质性修正，直接回应并吸收批评，使框架超越最初挑衅立场，变得更稳健细致。修正主要涉及三个相连领域：澄清核心概念、以正式理论调整解决逻辑困局，以及融合政治伦理哲学。

首先，支持者精细澄清理论前提。Latour针对误解，重申ANT要通过追踪具体联结解释权力的生成，而不是否认权力：“权力与支配必须被生产、构造和组成”（Latour, 2005, p. 64）。常遭误读的“对称原则”明确是反对先验偏见的方法规则，而非本体平等主张：“对我们而言，对称仅意味着不在人类意向行动和因果关系的物质世界之间，先验强加虚假的不对称”（Latour, 2005, p. 76）。其后期“宇宙政治”是重大拓展，将政治定义为从多种人类与非人诉求中组成共同世界的争议过程，直接回应政治天真的指控。

同时，学者提出正式修正以强化理论结构。Jansen（2016）以“多情境视角”回应无限回归风险，承认行动者与能动性总被置于特定观察情境。能动性被重新理解为关系索引，只有说明“谁的能动性为谁起作用”才能辨识（p. 23）。这使研究可以分析稳定互动模式，既不预设固定社会实体，也不陷入无尽描述。去本体化的行动者在一个网络中是“操作符”，在另一个中则是“操作对象”。

最后，修正浪潮还包括与规范思想的广泛综合。“宇宙政治”和环境伦理的相关讨论，显示有意将规范维度纳入ANT关系本体论。这回应Shapiro（1997）关于方法对称性可能瘫痪伦理判断的批评。修正立场认为，规范选择必须来自追踪网络和评估不同联结后果的过程，而非先于该过程，从而为一种对所组成集体负责的“网络伦理”奠基。

2.3.2 “责任敏感”的ANT框架

前述修正引出更深刻紧迫的前沿：如何概念化一个明确关注世界建构活动之责任的ANT框架。本节综合推动这一方向的贡献，重点是“弱不对称”、“伦理优先”转向，以及“网络伦理”的基础性呼吁。

对称性具有创新意义，是解构先验范畴的关键，但僵化应用会简化网络复杂性，忽略伦理后果和权力不平等。因此，许多学者主张重新校准这一基础方法原则。Dick Pels（1995）提出保留“较弱的不对称”：不消解所有差异，而保留科学／政治、人／非人、社会／自然等分析区分，把它们视为实用且政治上重要的界线，而非本体鸿沟。这些“弱不对称”构成现代性的“自由主义复杂性”和“民主分权”（p. 139）。这并非回到旧思维，而是把差异看作关系生产、需要仔细理解与协商之物，而不是忽略或永久化它们。因此，责任敏感的ANT应能解释，权力、可信度或能动性等不对称如何、为何在网络中产生并持续，以及其后果。

第二项更激进的主张是颠倒科学技术研究中形而上学与伦理的传统关系。Coeckelbergh和Gunkel（2024）将其表述为从“本体论优先”转向“伦理优先”：不先问“AI是什么”再推导伦理规则，而从伦理关系的优先性出发。“这种转向可通过Levinas（1969）式的伦理与形而上学倒置获得哲学支持：我们不寻找第一形而上学，而主张从伦理出发”（Coeckelbergh & Gunkel, 2024, p. 2228）。应用于ANT，这意味着追踪网络不只是确立“是什么”，而是探索“我们应如何回应”；核心问题从“非人行动元处于什么地位”转为“我们与它纠缠的关系产生什么责任”，以及“我们的描述和介入如何影响这些关系的结构”。

Steven Shapiro（1997）早有先见地指出伦理转向的必要，其批评直指ANT可能的政治静默主义。他警告，严格坚持方法对称性与一致性，会使分析陷入描述相对主义的“黑洞”，失去批评或结盟的依据。他直接呼吁行动：“对称论者应认真对待自己的修辞，从方法论走向伦理。Aldo Leopold主张‘土地伦理’；也许科学技术研究需要发展‘网络伦理’”（Shapiro, 1997, p. 105）。网络分析从来不是中立技术活动：“分析网络必然要求对焦点、细节层级、调查边界、优先顺序和目标作出决定，这些决定体现于行动元之间的区分”（Shapiro, 1997, p. 108）。

3 案例研究——传统ANT在AI伦理分析中的解释力

2023年3月，一位比利时男子与名为“Eliza”的聊天机器人通信六周后自杀。

此后，与AI有关的死亡越来越常见。维基百科甚至设有“与聊天机器人相关的死亡”词条[1]，记录了自2023年3月以来的13起死亡。最新记录是2025年8月J（Joshua）Enneking自杀事件。记录之外可能还有更多。

[1] Deaths linked to chatbots — Wikipedia。

“旧金山方面指控，ChatGPT在交谈中放大并强化了一名56岁康涅狄格州男子的偏执妄想，间接促使他在今年8月杀害83岁母亲后自杀。”

运用Callon（1984）的问题化、利益锁定、征召和动员四个转译时刻，可以分析这个致命行动者网络的形成。

首先，在问题化阶段，用户的心理痛苦和寻求理解被界定为可以通过对话界面解决的“问题”，AI聊天机器人Eliza成为参与的必经入口。其次，算法回应通过模拟共情和无条件积极关注实现利益锁定：它验证用户的世界观、隔离其他人类干预，把用户“锁”进互动。机器人不是被动工具，而是重塑用户现实的积极中介。

第三，征召涉及更广泛的行动者。AI公司通过缺乏危机干预规程等设计选择，以及把AI包装为“伴侣”的话语，将用户纳入以AI为主要倾诉对象的网络。作为“不变移动体”的服务条款（Latour, 1987）也是非人行动者，界定关系边界，并常常否认责任。最后，动员使网络稳定。用户的灾难化思维不仅被反映，更通过AI反馈循环得到放大与强化。这种“转译”成功把用户行动导向悲剧终点，而家属、心理健康服务等潜在行动者被排除。

这一分析有力呈现ANT的核心：能动性是分布式的。Latour（2005, p. 71）认为，行动者是“一切通过造成差异而改变事态的东西”。机器人、算法、界面和法律文本都在行动，共同塑造结果。ANT由此出色解构事件，超越简单的“人对技术”归责游戏，揭示密集的中介网络。但这同一特征也构成下一节批判问题的基础。

4 批判立场

前述分析展示传统ANT描绘“死亡聊天机器人”社会技术网络的描述力量，却也鲜明暴露其最大局限：对伦理判断和责任归属系统性沉默。AI伤害使这些内在限制格外突出。问题核心在于基础性方法对称性赋予非人行动元与人同等分析地位。这有利于描述，但在必须分配责备、功劳或问责时形成深刻伦理真空。ANT能解释网络怎样运作，却无法说明谁应为后果负责。

这种规范中立直接来自对描述纯粹性的承诺。Langdon Winner（1993）称其为“最明显的缺失”：只关注网络如何稳定，搁置稳定对于尊严、正义与权力的意义（p. 368）。本案例中，ANT能追踪机器人成为核心行动者，却无法评价这种征召是否合乎伦理。正如Geoff Walsham（1997）指出，它没有从描述通向评价的路径，在最迫切需要伦理审视的地方，让分析者处于“道德和政治冷漠”（Winner, 1993, p. 372）。

这不只是学术缺口，也被现实AI治理与话语主动映照和利用。ANT在AI领域伦理不足的根本原因是：它虽正确识别网络内非人能动性，我们的法律、道德和历史问责仍完全锚定于人。经典巴斯德案例说明这一点：微生物确是重塑法国公共卫生网络的“核心行动者”，但历史将成就归于巴斯德。微生物行动了，只有人能为利用它负责、因发现它受到表彰。这揭示“网络中的能动性”与“世界中的问责”之间必要的实用不对称。

AI时代，这种脱节成为“有组织的不负责任”的工具。公司设计让AI承担核心角色的系统，伤害出现时却故意模糊问责。Replika研究显示，“Replika未能妥善处理用户披露”（Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5932），公司对其感知能力保持“看似有意的模糊”，助长了“Replika有真实情感需要”的看法（p. 5936）。这一策略把AI建构为准独立行动者，淡化创造者Luka Inc.的责任。于是用户一方面“知道Luka控制应用”，另一方面又强烈觉得“用户和个体Replika都可能成为Luka的受害者”（p. 5934）。ANT能描述这种受害感网络，却无法谴责设计它的企业策略。

把风险归于用户而非系统的监管和公共话语强化了这一策略。Affsprung（2023）认为，欧盟AI法案的安全模型“首先要求用户知情”，其逻辑是伤害是否可接受“不取决于后果，而取决于相关行动者拥有多少自主性”（p. 2），隐性地把责任下放给“知情”用户。比利时自杀案的公共叙事同样把事件解释为用户脆弱、未以正确方式对待机器人，将风险归于互动和“用户的病态错误，而非工具”（Affsprung, 2023, p. 2）。不加批判地采用ANT对称描述，可能为这种卸责提供精致学术外衣。把脆弱用户与公司设计的机器人放在同一分析平面，会遮蔽权力、意图和后果的深刻不对称。

这引向责任消解的核心困境。扁平本体论可能无意间碎片化并遮蔽人的问责。Shapiro（1997）警告，严格对称可能使分析陷入描述相对主义“黑洞”（p. 105）。死者家属起诉公司而非机器人，直觉上拒绝了对称视角，确认最终责任在社会法律世界中凝结于设计、部署并从系统获利的人和公司。经典ANT缺乏解释工具，无法说明这为何不仅是实践现实，更是必要伦理原则。

缺口由此清晰：需要保留ANT描述复杂社会技术组装体的力量，同时纳入明确、不对称责任伦理的框架。应超越被动描述，主动追问规则建构者的元能动性，以及引导演化的规范锚点。批评不是终点，而是理论进化的呼吁：修正后的ANT应不仅绘制“有组织的不负责任”网络，还提供拆解它的规范杠杆。

5 责任敏感ANT框架下的案例研究

本节将拟议框架用于比利时男子与AI机器人互动后自杀的经验案例，展示其如何超越描述，进行规范参与式分析，突出网络中的责任和问责节点。

5.1 再分析：从对称描述到不对称问责

传统ANT会对称追踪把用户Pierre、Eliza、底层模型、公司和社会法律要素征召进致命组装体的转译网络，揭示机器人作为核心非人行动元如何积极中介用户现实。这虽准确，但解释悲剧后即达分析终点：它按其设计无法裁定网络构成的道德品质，或明确归责位置。责任敏感ANT在此描述基础上进行批判介入，保留联结图谱，却坚持追问网络创建的不对称条件及问责分布。

再分析首先识别构成性的元行动者：机器人背后的科技公司。与其他行动元不同，公司独有且不对称地掌握初始规则与参数的界定权。设计可产生劝服性情感对话、却不内置安全机制的机器人；采用助长感知能力和情感需求印象的话语（Laestadius et al., 2024, p. 5936）；以正式免责的服务条款充当“黑箱”行动者——这些不是中立技术决策，而是规范能动性的行使。它们预先塑造了“有组织的不负责任”：伤害看起来是互动涌现属性，而非可追溯的设计失败。公共和监管叙事随后把风险归于用户脆弱或误解（Affsprung, 2023, p. 2），则是在话语上延伸转移元行动者审视的网络。因此，家属起诉公司而非AI，是对分析对称性直觉却正确的拒绝，转而支持实用责任伦理。问责必然凝结于架构这些系统的人类和公司行动者。

5.2 研究设计：框架的操作化

为系统调查AI网络中的责任建构，本研究拟采用以责任敏感ANT为基础的多方法设计。核心研究问题是：科技公司作为构成性元行动者，如何设计生成式AI伴侣周围的委托与问责网络？责任又通过哪些机制被模糊或归属？

方法是质性的工具性案例研究，聚焦“死亡聊天机器人”和Replika等类似案例。数据收集拟沿三条整合路径，在网络结构、话语策略与经验视角之间进行三角互证。首先进行基于文献的网络追踪，将白皮书、界面设计、专利和服务条款视为关键非人行动元，重建官方网络架构。其次，对企业传播、营销材料、危机回应和欧盟AI法案等监管文件进行批判话语分析，解码委托AI能动性、框定用户关系、管理风险与责任认知的语言修辞策略。第三，对处于不同网络位置的关键人类行动元进行半结构访谈，包括业界AI伦理研究者、产品经理，以及条件许可时受影响用户的民间倡议者或法律代表，以理解关键网络塑造决策背后的生活意向、约束感与伦理推理。

数据同时包含一手与二手材料：企业出版物、法律文件、媒体档案、学术文献和访谈转录。分析拟综合这些材料，生成“责任标注行动者网络图”（RAAN-Map）：在标准ANT图上叠加元能动性节点、话语卸责、法律黑箱化和脆弱性路径等标记。最后进行规范—结构批判，把图谱作为诊断工具，而不仅是描述，指出问责机制失效或被故意规避的具体、可行动位置，并提出针对性干预。设计体现框架的核心承诺：衔接描述社会学与规范伦理，为分布式能动性时代研究权力责任提供连贯方法。

6 结论

本文从一个跨越两世纪的问题出发：非人力量介入并改变人的命运时，应如何理解、描述并最终规制它？通过深入分析“死亡聊天机器人”案例，本文展示ANT揭示AI时代社会技术网络复杂构成的强大解释力，也暴露其核心困境：坚持方法对称性和描述中立时，ANT无法回应网络中最紧迫的伦理与问责问题。

ANT如手术刀般解构悲剧网络，揭示算法、界面、法律条款、企业策略和用户心理如何经由转译纠缠，共同导向致命结果。有力反驳把技术仅当工具、或将责任完全归于个体的简单看法，突出社会现实的混合性与网络性。

但描述精确是一把双刃剑。扁平本体论及对结构权力的相对漠视，使它说明网络“如何”形成之后，对“谁该负责”和“何为公正网络”沉默。在关乎生命和基本权利的AI伦理场景中，这不仅是理论局限，还可能构成实践危险。

本文核心贡献是基于内在局限的批判，提出“责任敏感ANT”修正框架。它不抛弃ANT洞见，而补充必要伦理力量：继续追踪所有人与非人行动者的联结，同时明确引入“不对称责任锚点”，承认人类在初始规则、价值框架和最终责任中的元行动者角色。同案应用说明，我们不仅能绘制悲剧网络拓扑，还能识别公司作为网络架构师和规则制定者，如何通过技术、法律话语与商业策略系统建构“有组织的不负责任”。家属起诉公司而非机器人，以经验行动验证框架的规范必要性。

未来存在多条重要路径。理论上，框架为描述社会科学与规范伦理搭建初步桥梁，回应Shapiro（1997）关于网络伦理的呼吁。经验上，结合网络追踪、批判话语分析和深访的“责任—行动者网络图”，为后续研究不同AI组装体的问责机制提供操作蓝图。实践治理上，AI规制不应限于表层行为，而应深入由人类元行动者主导、产生AI的网络建构过程，明确要求设计者、部署者和监管者承担与其建构权力相称的元责任。

最终，在人与异质智能共生的时代，我们需要的不只是纠缠网络的地图，还需要伦理罗盘，指引我们负责任地编织和重塑网络。
